speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to participate in this discussion for a few moments. First, I would like to suggest that from the very clear question that was put at the opening of this debate and the reply given by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), my understanding is that the matter is not before the courts now but that it had been before the courts back in September of last year. It is certainly not before the courts now, and if it is, then obviously his answer was more than evasive.
The important thing we want to discuss today is the merits of the case within the framework and atmosphere in which we deal with these things. I do not think that there is any doubt in my mind or the mind of any other Member of Parliament who comes to the National Capital Region that public servants by and large should be given full political rights, rights which they have not had in the past. I say that because we are all too familiar with public servants who do work on our election
Public Service
campaigns and, if we believe the interpretation of the Public Service Commission, are working on our election campaigns illegally. I would feel very sorry for any Canadian citizen who is involved in a political process if that citizen is classified as doing something illegal. I do feel that this is a subject which we should and will deal with in the not too distant future.
The important thing we must consider is that in the last 12 years I have been here, and particularly in the last five or six years, this matter has been discussed more and more openly. A momentum and consensus have been building up among members of all Parties that the public servants should be given full political freedoms and that if they are disallowed from having those full political freedoms at this time, then the law should be changed.
Having said that, I would draw to the attention of the House the remarks already drawn to attention by the previous two speakers, point number four in a letter put out by the leader of the Progressive Conservative Party last August during the election campaign. It has already been read into the record but it indicates that the Progressive Conservative Party favours a general removal of restrictions on political activities for public servants. That clearly states my concern, and I think our Party's concern, for carrying on this process and opening up the political arena to those people who are public servants. I say that with the knowledge that I had some involvement in the phrasing and writing of this article which came out as part of our Party's platform on public servants.
I say that also because perhaps I bring a different point of view to this issue in that I am perhaps the only person in this Chamber who was a public servant who got fired because he sought a federal nomination. Having lost my job over that and feeling, some 12 or 13 years ago, that it was unfair and unjust and having taken it to the Divisional Court and three years later received my response, I must admit that I have always felt that I opted out by not taking the matter further to the Supreme Court of Canada. However, at the time it did not seem that important since I was already through my second federal election campaign before the Divisional Court of Ontario dealt with the matter. There is a reported decision on that matter in the law books.
I personally felt very strongly about this issue at a time when the few dollars that were involved were very, very crucial to my well-being and that of my family. I have not lessened my interest in the topic. However, I ask all Members to consider that the Party of which I happen to be a member, the Party which forms the Government of the day, did make that promise during the last election campaign along with a number of other promises.
Seven months is not a very long period of time. We have implemented quite a few of the commitments that were made during the election campaign, and those commitments are not being introduced and passed within the first six months willy-nilly. One could not possibly, in a well organized and planned program, introduce all the commitments which a Party makes in an election campaign within six months. We have a four-year term, and throughout those four years, I hope that all

April 15, 1985
Public Service
those commitments will be introduced, passed and become the order of the day in this country. Not all can be dealt with during the first six months leaving three and a half years before we implement any other programs. I think that they should be balanced over a period of time.
Having said that, since we are a federal Government looking at a federal situation, I do not see why we should be rushing into this matter within the first six or seven months. It has been a long-standing sore and I do not believe that it has to be wiped out in six months.
Having said that, 1 would like to point out, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) who introduced the motion stated, that the Government has not been sitting back and doing nothing. The Government has begun to negotiate with the unions. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) is discussing this matter with the unions at the present time.
That is exactly what the Government said about the fourth point. The Government feels that the people who are in the bargaining units should be relieved of the illegality of this matter. Because the Government is currently bargaining with the unions, I feel that it is inappropriate to bring the matter forward in other forums. However, in many situations negotiations are very touchy and I do not want to build up false hopes. In addition, I certainly hope that no Member would use this forum to obtain a political advantage during the provincial election campaign. That would be demagoguery. I hope that Members have the better interests of federal public servants in mind, in order that this matter can be resolved before the next federal election.
This Government is the first Government which has taken the step to put the matter on the bargaining table, and I believe the Government should be commended for that initial step. However, if for some reason the topic is not resolved during the negotiations with an agreement arrived at which excludes the topic of political rights for public servants, we will still have about three-and-a-half years left in this term to deal with the issue. The issue could be resolved by way of a motion, by the route which was suggested by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), by striking a special committee in the House, or by way of a Private Member's Bill. I would whole-heartedly support the other means by which this matter could be brought forward for full discussion at a later stage. However, I believe it is important to allow the current negotiating process to continue.
Several matters were raised, such as a person putting a sign on his front lawn. In such case I would ask the person if they owned the house in joint tenancy, and if so, the sign should be put on an appropriate portion of the front lawn. Most people own their homes in joint tenancy and I do not think that the Public Service Commission would get excited about that situation. If it does-and if it is of value-I would offer my services free of charge to defend that person. However, such person might want to pay for services and get someone more skilled
than I am in the courts. I have not been in the courts for a long period of time. But, I do feel strongly about the matter.
The guidelines which were published during the last election campaign by the Public Service Commission had never before been published in such a hard-nosed, definitive and brutal manner. During the previous four election campaigns in which I had been a candidate the matter was not as controversial as it became during the last election campaign. I felt that the Public Service Commission took a very insensitive and dogmatic position, which both surprised and concerned me. However, that action may have crystalized the point and brought it into focus. Because of its actions, the Public Service Commission has now joined the debate.
I do not think there is anything else that can be said at this time. Along with Members from all sides of the House, 1 support the aim, intention and goal of ensuring that public servants, at least those in the bargaining units, have the full rights of all other Canadians in the political process of Canada. I am not convinced, however, that bringing up this matter at the present time is furthering that end. I believe it is unfortunate that the matter was brought up at this time when negotiations are ongoing. I hope those negotiations are successful. Should they not bear the fruit which I optimistically hope they will bear, then I believe the matter should come before the House and subsequently go to committee to be dealt with at that time.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF GRANTING RIGHT TO POLITICAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the political rights of public servants are an issue which is very close to my heart. In my opinion, Canadians who earn their living as public servants have the right to act as full-fledged citizens, and choosing a government and exercising one's franchise are of course some of the rights of full-fledged citizens. I am therefore very happy that we are discussing this subject today, but I would like the issue of the rights of civil servants to be dealt with and not just the matter of a few isolated political rights which it may seem appropriate at this time to give back to public servants without taking into account the whole context in which federal public servants operate in Canada.

We know, for instance, that political neutrality is an essential requirement in the federal Public Service, particularly in retaining its credibility with the democratic society which it serves.
The question is, if the restrictions which are currently in place are diminished, what else can we put in place to ensure the political neutrality of the public service? We must address the question of political rights by looking at five elements.
We must look at the question from the point of view of Parliament. We know that the historical interests of Parliament have stemmed from the need to remove the influence of the Crown from the electoral process. A related concern of both parliamentarians and Ministers is that officials should
April 15, 1985

not use their public positions to promote their personal political philosophies. Such conduct, rightly, is seen as a contravention of democratic politics. Also, Ministers share many of the same concerns as parliamentarians. They have an additional interest, namely, that they should be assured that the advice which they receive is not motivated by partisan or other types of political considerations. They must also be assured, in the execution of decisions and the administration of policies, that their officials act in good faith.
The Public Service, which aspires to serve Governments of different political complexions, has an interest which is complementary to that of Ministers. Its own rationale depends on being perceived as the impartial servant of the Government that holds office. It is correspondingly important that the public should not feel that political allegiancies enter into or affect their dealings with government agencies. Therefore, the Public Service has an interest in ensuring that its professionalism is protected in whatever rules and regulations apply to the exercise of political rights. We must determine where the rights of public servants meet those of the public.
Individual public servants are affected mainly if they wish to exercise political rights. That has become increasingly visible as the Public Service has increased in number. However, as has been pointed out by previous speakers, there are many public servants who perform routine functions that are not inherently governmental. It seems illogical not to permit those individuals greater political freedom than individuals whose sole service to Government is to give advice on policy, or who have a direct interface with the public on a day to day basis. In those cases, the individuals would find it very difficult to be objective, as they are deeply involved in the political choices.
We must also know that the public interest is diverse as well. The public must be assured that political allegiance is not a factor in the dealings it has with government departments and agencies. It will expect advancement in the Public Service to be on grounds of merit and efficiency, not on political inclination.
That brings up the whole matter of the merit system and the business of intervention within the professional Public Service which has gone on in the past decade and which has diminished the professionalism of the Civil Service. It has created many problems for certain civil servants who wanted to give objective advice but felt the pressure imposed upon them, perhaps by a superior or colleague who seemed to have been appointed rather than having arrived at this position of authority through simple merit and competence.
Therefore, if we are going to look at the political rights of civil servants, we must also look at the merit principle in the Civil Service. We must ensure that the public servant is protected between elections from pressures being put on him or her to give advice which is other than objective and professional. I believe that is as important an element as that of extending political rights to civil servants. We cannot look at increasing one set of political rights without looking at the
Public Service
responsibilities, the climate and the environment in which these public servants must work.
The Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle which completed its review in 1979, stated, and I quote:
With respect to public servants who perform a regulatory role, many interven-ors stated that these public servants should not be given freedom to participate in party politics. Otherwise, the public might well perceive that a licence denial had political connotations when, in fact, it stemmed from failure to meet the requirements for granting of a licence.
That is one example which is given by the special committee. It continues:
The theme of most intervenors who took this position was that, when public servants are in direct contact with the general public, they must be seen to be politically neutral.
Government must be perceived to serve the public and to serve the public good. Public servants in the employ of the Government must also be professional and be perceived by the public as serving its interests first and foremost. It cannot make any discrimination on the basis of age, sex, race, religion or political belief.
I believe that when we look at the political rights of civil servants, we must also remember the ultimate right of every citizen to receive objective service for the taxes they pay to the treasury every year. In addition, Government has a basic concern with the concept of public interest. It must deliver services directed toward the public good and needs impartial employees.
In determining the extent to which public servants should be permitted to participate in the political process, we must endeavour to strike a balance between the individual's rights and freedoms enshrined in the Canadian Charter and at least two other very important rights, namely, the right of the Government to receive objective information and impartial advice based on professional expertise, and the right of the Canadian public to be confident that its public servants deliver the Government's services in a professional and impartial manner. Any relaxation of the current rules should not compromise these principles. Any changes in the current legislative provisions must not be undertaken before the impact of the long-term consequences for the Government, the Canadian people and the Public Service itself has been thoroughly explored.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-CANADA-UNITED STATES DISCUSSIONS. (B) NIAGARA RIVER POLLUTION
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-CANADA-UNITED STATES DISCUSSIONS. (B) NIAGARA RIVER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in raising the question of acid rain in March, with the then upcoming conference in Quebec City, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gave me a quite explicit and articulate demonstration of his capacity for public relations and empty promises, as well as an attempt to rewrite Canadian history in the field of acid rain. The commitment made at the time was that Canada would be strong and active on the national and international scene in defence of Canada's acid rain concerns and our desire to progressively cut acid rain in order to protect our lakes, forests, agriculture, our health, and industry in general. Therefore, the initiative taken last week by the eastern Canadian premiers and the governors of the New England States is to be commended. Actually it should be expanded to include western Canadian premiers and the governors of the U.S. west coast States.
However, what I find distressing, in light of the rhetoric of the Prime Minister last March, is who was not there in Quebec City. It turns out that the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) was not there. Not only was she not there, but also the acid rain envoy, former Premier Bill Davis, was not there. Their absence, of course, created some concern as to how serious Canada is on this issue; if it does not find the time to send its spokesperson on the environment and the new Canadian envoy on acid rain to watch the proceedings and take up the issues as they are raised during that kind of event.
I refer specifically to that old red herring raised by Governor Sununu of New Hampshire. He is famous for saying that Canadians on a per capita basis produce more acid rain than the Americans do. He then leaves the impression that it is a one-sided type of responsibility which rests entirely on our shoulders. Of course, the truth is far from that.
April 15, 1985

Of course, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) was there to defend the Canadian position, and 1 commend him. But the Minister of the Environment was not there and, because of her knowledge of the subject and the input she would have been able to make, she could have taken on Governor Sununu and told him, look, my friend, this is not the politics of per capita, this the politics of who is downwind to whom and who is producing more substance upwind from the other.
The facts are that while Canada produces some 4.6 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide a year, the U.S. produces almost six times as much or 26 million tonnes a year and we are downwind to them. That is an argument that Mr. Sununu did not hear in New Hampshire. He should have heard it from the Minister of the Environment. Instead, he went home with a notion that he had somehow scored some points.
He also did not hear that in Canada we at least have a reduction program in place which provides for cuts of 25 per cent in our sulphur dioxide emissions between 1980 and 1990. The U.S. does not have such a program in place. Furthermore, we have a very important political commitment of an additional 25 per cent cut in SOI 2 emissions by 1994, so that the total cut will be 50 per cent. Again, Mr. Sununu goes home after no one was there to give him this kind of message on behalf of the federal Government.
One could continue on this theme but it would be at the risk of giving Governor Sununu too much importance. However, it is important that we do not leave it up to Americans like Professor Eville Gorham, Professor of Ecology at the University of Minnesota, to come to Canada's defence. He is reported in The Citizen as saying at the end of the day that Governor Sununu's statement was quite unfriendly and unwarranted. That is a fact.
I will conclude because I also would like to know what the Government is planning to do in the next few months, during the period leading to the Helsinki Agreement when a protocol will be signed by the EEC nations, Canada, the Nordic nations and most of the Western and Eastern European nations, committing themselves to a cut of a minimum of 30 per cent by 1993. I submit that this is the time for Canada to become very active on the international scene and to put pressure on our friends south of the border.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-CANADA-UNITED STATES DISCUSSIONS. (B) NIAGARA RIVER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to clarify something the Liberal environment critic said. We were in fact very well represented in Quebec City. Several officials of my Department attended the meeting organized by the Quebec Government and the Northeastern American states. In addition, my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser), who is a former Minister of the Environment, and therefore
Adjournment Debate
quite familiar with this issue, was well able to put forward the Canadian position, which he did with great distinction.
Naturally, I was not in Quebec City, Mr. Speaker, as this meeting had first been scheduled for the month of March but that date was later changed to April by the Quebec Government and I had already planned discussions at that time with my OECD counterparts in Paris and in Stockholm, where I met with many ministers and looked at how Sweden protects its environment. As Hon. Members are aware, that country was the first to create a Department of the Environment and it was at the invitation of the Swedish Government that I visited there. I was not on holidays, as it was maliciously suggested.
What surprises me, Mr. Speaker, is that the environment critic finds all his information in the newspapers, and often not in the best ones. If there were a newspaper strike tomorrow, I believe he would be unable to ask any questions in the House. 1 would really feel quite sorry for him.
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to tell you what our Government has done about acid rain. Contrary to what the environment critic suggested, the federal Government has made a lot of progress in its fight against acid rain. We have implemented a program to reduce emissions from Canadian sources of acid rain and guaranteed financial support to the foundries which are unable to pay for anti-pollution devices themselves. We have guaranteed financial assistance for research, monitoring programs and the development of new clean-up technologies. We have announced very strict emission standards for automobiles and light trucks.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, we have a most comprehensive policy to fight acid rain at the present time, and I believe that this Government, which has succeeded in implementing this policy and concerted approach within six months of its coming to power, should be commended and not constantly criticized by my hon. colleague, the former Minister of the Environment, who would like us to believe that the previous Government did much in the environmental field, even though it did nothing: the only comprehensive policy to have ever been implemented in Canada is basically the one developed by this Government.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-INCLUSION OF SEVERANCE PAY IN INCOME CALCULATION. (B) EFFECT ON LAID-OFF WORKERS

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on March 22, 26, again on April 1, and earlier in the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration, I tried to put questions to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) with respect to her proposal to include severance pay as income under the Unemployment Insurance Act. This would mean that those people who were given severance pay when they were dismissed from their jobs would have to use that severance pay to

April 15, 1985
Adjournment Debate
cover the basic necessities of life because unemployment insurance would be delayed.
What does this mean? It means that a lot of people who would otherwise roll over that severance pay into a pension plan, who would use that severance pay to move to another place in Canada where there were better employment opportunities, who would use that severance pay to set themselves up in a business and to re-establish themselves in employment, would not be able to do it any longer because they would have to use that money for the basic needs of life.
1 asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration whether she had made any impact studies before introducing these matters. 1 got no answer. I asked her to delay the implementation of the program which was to go in effect on April 1 so she could consult and do impact studies. Again she refused. As a matter of fact the only answer I got was that she did in fact have consultations. She wondered why I took so long in putting questions to her about this subject, that 1 only started in March. I might say that I was in touch with her office much sooner by telephone and by letter but I only started raising the subject in March in committee, that is correct.
The Minister put those questions to me. I must ask her whether she gives the same answer to all those people who are writing letters to us. Did she say that to the people who raised this issue at her own economic summit called by the Conservative Government when two-thirds of the people at that summit signed a petition asking for a delay? Did she insult them as well and ask why they were only raising the matter at that time? The Toronto Star only raised it in an editorial on April 13.
I have example after example here of people who raised this matter only in the month of March and later even the Government. 1 have a memo leaked to me by an official in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. This is a memo from one of the directors of staff relations to all regional personnel managers. He said that several queries concerning the treatment of severance pay for unemployment insurance benefits have prompted the following explanation of the proposed changes that will "probably" be implemented March 31, 1985. Although we have not received official notification of the changes, we have contacted CEIC representatives and obtained the following information". That memo was dated March 12, 1985. In that department they still had not received any information.
Then there is the bulletin of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada-this is in the middle of March. It states that it regrets having to provide only an unofficial interpretation of these important changes. Along with other public service unions, the Professional Institute has requested a delay in the implementation of the changes to allow further studies. To date, however, it had not received a reply to that request or an official interpretation from Treasury Board.
All kinds of people were confused by these announcements, and rightly so. The Minister said these were announced on November 8. All we had announced on November 8 by the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was a short paragraph on page 13 of his speech which said:
In order to make the (U.I.C.) program more effective and less costly, a number of adminsitrativc changes related to the determination of eligibility for benefits will be made.
In the Blue Book tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) it states simply, "separation payments-employment and immigration-$60 million-separation payments are not considered to be earned income when eligibility for unemployment insurance is determined". That is all. It is obvious that it took a lot of people a lot of time to find out what are the implications of this decision to make severance pay income for unemployment insurance purposes. People only began to see the implications after the Christmas recess, and they then started to write us letters. Because of that, when we saw what the implications were, we started to escalate our questions to the Minister asking for a delay. What was originally only a very sketchy program became a very complicated one.

The Minister accused me of loafing around, not doing my job earlier, or not putting questions to her in December. It is interesting to note that it was only on March 29 that the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission announced approval of regulatory changes in the treatment of severance payments for unemployment insurance. The regulations were only adopted in late March. Then on December 21, the only other notice we had following the November 8 statement, the day on which we adjourned for Christmas, the Minister issued a press release saying that the implementation date for the treatment of severance payments would be March 31, 1985.
How much consultation did she do in the period from November 8 to December 21 on this important issue? The Parliamentary Secretary is here. He is an honest man. I know he will table for us today all groups, unions and employee groups that were consulted on this matter. I hope they were not just ones the Minister hand-picked. 1 hope she did a very thorough consultative job in the six weeks to which I referred. I should like the Parliamentary Secretary to tell us who in fact the Minister consulted with on the implementation of this program. Let us have the names of the people and the organizations.
The Minister has already admitted that there were no impact studies. She said that the Minister of Finance should have done impact studies. The Minister of Finance said that they should have been done by the Minister of Employment. However, none were done. This is a very serious program which touches a lot of people. I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to tell us how many people it touches. Once more will he advise the Minister to delay this very harsh and very inequitable program?

speechtext:

league from Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) just said that I am an honest man, but perhaps he will be disappointed because honesty has nothing to do with reading off a long list of names of people who were consulted. As announced by the Minister, it was decided that the new rules woirld take effect on March 31. The Act has been amended, unemployment benefits will be delayed or reduced in accordance with benefits paid when employment ends. These benefits include severance pay, earned paid leave, bonuses, gratuities, salary paid in lieu of advance notice, vacation leave and retroactive pay. The purpose of these important changes is to make sure that all employment income is treated the same way under the Unemployment Insurance Plan. They will eliminate compensations from two sources while maintaining all the benefits of the program, namely, the replacement of lost income while avoiding double payments.
On the other hand, to ensure fairness between the old legislation and the new one, a whole series of programs have been announced to allow people who had negotiated agreements in good faith following collective bargainings or a plant closing, because the problem had come to light between November 8 and December 21 as a result of consultations or questions within our caucus and from both sides of the House. The interim measures announced on December 21 will apply from March 31, 1985, and in the case of retirees, from January 1, 1986.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-PREMIER'S TRIAL-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF MARIJUANA FIND. (B) DATE INQUIRY
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-PREMIER'S TRIAL-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF MARIJUANA FIND. (B) DATE INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 4 I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) when he first advised the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that marijuana was allegedly found in the luggage of Premier Hatfield. I had asked the question on a number of other occasions. I was not given an answer by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) or the Solicitor General. I put the question to the Solicitor General on March 4. Rather than the Solicitor General standing up to answer the question, the Minister of Justice stood up. It was somewhat strange that the Minister of Justice should stand to defend the Solicitor General when only a week and a half before he indicated that had he been in Opposition he would have asked for the resignation of the Solicitor General for his deplorable and disgraceful secret
Adjournment Debate
meeting with Premier Hatfield at the Chateau Laurier on October 7. 1 asked when the Prime Minister was first advised. The Minister of Justice stood up and indicated that the Prime Minister was told the day before charges were laid. The charges were laid on October 26. The Minister of Justice told this House that the Prime Minister first became aware of the fact that marijuana was found in Premeir Hatfield's luggage on October 25. That is utter nonsense. I hope that was not a deliberate attempt to mislead the House, but in fact it was a deliberate misstatement of fact. I would like to state why.
The marijuana was found on September 25, 1984. The Solicitor General indicated that he was first made aware on September 26 that the marijuana was found. He indicated that the Commissioner of the RCMP advised him of that fact.
On October 20, 1984 the Fredericton Gleaner ran a major story, indicating that a senior New Brunswick politician was being investigated for a particular drug offence. At that point in time it was not known who this senior New Brunswick politician was. That was October 20. On October 22, Premier Hatfield held a press conference to indicate that it was he who was under investigation. He also declared his innocence in the matter. It was national news from coast to coast. It was reported in every newspaper in this country. On every radio station and television station that marijuana was found in Premier Hatfield's luggage. That was on October 22. We have the Minister of Justice telling us in this House and the Canadian people that the Prime Minister was not aware of the fact that marijuana was found until October 25, the day before charges were laid.
One can see how ludicrous and misleading that statement was. By making that statement, the Minister of Justice was suggesting that the Prime Minister was closeted somewhere for three days, without access to newspapers, television or radio, that he was totally unaware of what was going on in this country. 1 indicated that it was utter nonsense. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will stand in the House today to apologize to this House and the Canadian people with respect to when the Prime Minister was first made aware that marijuana was found.
It is curious why the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General refused to be forthcoming with respect to this incident. We in the Liberal Party, the Official Opposition, have been concerned from the very start that there has been a very basic breach of that fundamental principle of our criminal justice system, that all persons be treated equally before the law. This Government is involved in stonewalling. It refuses to be forthright and refuses to give us answers to the very necessary questions that are being asked as a result of the so-called MacKay-Hatfield affair. One can only conclude that the Government, the Prime Minister, the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice have something to hide.
We in the Opposition have consistently asked for an independent judicial inquiry into the whole matter to determine how extensive the political interference was. We know

April IS, 1985
Adjournment Debate
for a fact that the Solicitor General, on his own admission, met secretly with Premier Hatfield on October 7 at the Chateau Laurier to further discuss the case. The mere fact that he met with Premier Hatfield would suggest extremely poor judgment, not only on the part of the Solicitor General but also on the part of Premier Hatfield for asking for that particular meeting.
The point we in opposition have been trying to make is that it is basic and fundamental that all persons be treated equally before the law. It was clear to us that Premier Hatfield was given that audience with the Solicitor General because he was a Premier of a province. Had it been Joe Blow from Kokomo, or a poor teenager from the other side of the tracks in York South-Weston, he would not have been given an audience with the Solicitor General of Canada.
Members of the legal community are unanimous with respect to the propriety of the Solicitor General meeting secretly with Premier Hatfield. They say it was wrong, that it is not the role of the Solicitor General to personally involve himself in a criminal investigation. Members of the media are almost unanimous on the matter. They are unanimous in the belief that the Solicitor General exercised poor judgment. Some have gone so far as to call for his resignation. The Solicitor General has refused to resign. He is continually clinging to power.
At this point, we are waiting for the internal RCMP report which was promised us weeks and weeks ago. We are hoping that it will come forward, and will give us the answers to those very basic questions for which we and the Canadian people have been waiting.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-PREMIER'S TRIAL-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF MARIJUANA FIND. (B) DATE INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 4 the Hon. Member asked the question which is the subject-matter of his comments today. At that time, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) said the following:
The reason 1 am rising to reply, Mr. Speaker, is that I informed the Prime Minister the day before the charges were laid that charges were to be laid against Premier Hatfield.
Since that time, to the best of my recollection, the Minister of Justice has appeared before the committee on the Estimates. The Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) has appeared twice, but in both cases, the hearings were terminated because of a vote in the House, although there was a brief opportunity for questioning. I know that the Solicitor General will be appearing on Estimates within the next week. The Hon. Member who has every right to pose whatever questions he sees fit with respect to this matter will have an opportunity to ask these questions of the Solicitor General. Indeed, he has such an opportunity every day in Question Period.
I do not intend to give hearsay upon hearsay today. All I can say is what I know the Minister of Justice has said, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was advised that charges were going to be laid against the Premier, and that that advice was given the day before charges were in fact laid.
